strengths: The paper addresses an important problem in EEG representation learning: creating a discrete, reusable tokenization scheme that is less tied to fixed channel configurations than many existing EEG models.

The proposed architecture is technically plausible and reasonably well motivated, combining STFT-based frequency modeling, raw temporal patches, VQ-style discretization, masked reconstruction, and masked token prediction in a coherent pipeline.
The empirical evaluation covers four clinically relevant EEG datasets and compares against several strong recent baselines, including BIOT and LaBraM, with results averaged over five random seeds.

The main performance tables show consistent gains across datasets and metrics, often with fewer parameters than competing models, which is encouraging evidence that the time-frequency tokenizer is useful.

The paper includes useful ablations on raw-only vs STFT-only vs joint modeling, masking strategy, vocabulary size, positional embeddings, and masked token prediction, which helps isolate some design choices.
The token visualization and retrieval analyses are a nice attempt to go beyond accuracy and examine whether the learned discrete codes carry interpretable or class-relevant information.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate rather than strong: the method largely combines established components, including STFT features, VQ-VAE-style quantization, transformer encoders, and masked token prediction. The paper could position more precisely what is fundamentally new beyond applying this recipe to EEG with frequency-aware masking.

The central claims about scalability and generalization are not fully supported. The experiments are mostly single-dataset training and evaluation, with no convincing cross-dataset transfer, cross-montage transfer, missing-channel robustness, or adaptation to genuinely different acquisition setups.

The evaluation of the tokenizer as a reusable foundation component is limited. The tokenizer appears to be trained within each dataset rather than learned once and transferred broadly, which weakens the claim of a general EEG tokenizer.

Several improvements are modest and sometimes within or near the reported standard deviations, especially on TUAB and some TUEV metrics. Statistical significance testing or clearer paired comparisons would be needed to support strong SOTA claims.

The interpretability analyses are suggestive but not rigorous. The class-token uniqueness metric is not clearly validated, can be sensitive to token frequency and class imbalance, and does not by itself establish clinical interpretability.

The frequency-learning analysis using spectral entropy of token sequences is questionable: applying Fourier analysis to sequences of discrete token IDs or token order does not straightforwardly measure whether the model captures physiologically meaningful frequency content.

Some important experimental details remain unclear, including whether unsupervised tokenizer pretraining ever uses validation/test data, how hyperparameter tuning was controlled across methods, and whether all baselines received comparable tuning budgets.

The paper claims reduced model footprint, but parameter accounting is somewhat confusing because tokenizers, encoders, and baseline pretraining components are not always counted in directly comparable ways.

The single-channel framing is attractive, but most downstream results still rely on multi-channel aggregation; the paper lacks direct evaluation on single-channel-only downstream settings or degraded-channel regimes.
Writing and presentation contain several typos, inconsistent naming between TFM-Token and TFM-Tokenizer, and some overclaimed statements, which slightly reduce clarity and confidence.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: scalable EEG representation learning with discrete tokenization and explicit time-frequency modeling.
The proposed architecture is reasonably coherent, combining STFT-based frequency patches, raw temporal patches, VQ-style tokenization, and masked-token encoder pretraining.
The paper evaluates on four clinically relevant EEG datasets and compares against several recent EEG baselines, including BIOT and LaBraM.
Includes useful ablations on raw-only vs STFT-only vs joint modeling, vocabulary size, masking strategy, position embeddings, and a plug-in experiment replacing LaBraM's tokenizer.
The method appears parameter-efficient relative to some baselines and achieves consistent reported gains across several metrics.
weaknesses: The central claims are substantially overstated. The work is framed as scalable/foundation-style EEG tokenization, but all training and pretraining are performed within each dataset; there is no convincing cross-dataset transfer, cross-task generalization, zero/few-shot adaptation, or channel-configuration robustness experiment.

Novelty is limited. The method is largely a combination of STFT features, transformer encoders, VQ-style codebooks, and masked modeling. The paper does not clearly distinguish what is technically new beyond applying these standard ingredients to EEG with a particular architecture.

Many reported improvements are modest and often comparable to the reported standard deviations. For example, TUEV balanced accuracy improves from about 0.468 to 0.494 with a standard deviation of 0.052, and no statistical significance testing or confidence analysis is provided.

The baseline comparison may not be fully fair or sufficiently controlled. LaBraM is evaluated with a different channel setup than its original design, parameter counts are discussed in ways that omit parts of competing systems, and it is unclear whether baselines received comparable hyperparameter tuning effort.

The evaluation does not isolate whether gains come from discretization, STFT preprocessing, architecture capacity, masked objectives, or tuning. The ablations are helpful but not decisive, and some comparisons conflate tokenizer design with encoder/training pipeline changes.

The token-quality analyses are weakly justified. The proposed class-token uniqueness metric is extremely low in absolute value, depends on labels despite unsupervised-tokenizer claims, and is not clearly connected to downstream usefulness. The retrieval and spectral-entropy analyses are suggestive but not rigorous.
The interpretability claim is under-supported. Visual inspection of a few highlighted tokens is anecdotal and does not establish clinically meaningful motifs or robust interpretability.

Some technical descriptions are confusing or imprecise, including the statement that quantization is applied 'along the time axis' rather than the embedding dimension, the rationale for omitting positional encodings due to EEG non-stationarity, and the exact tokenizer/codebook mechanics.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The paper gives many hyperparameters, but lacks sufficient implementation detail about preprocessing edge cases, code availability, compute cost, full tuning budgets, and whether validation/test handling avoids segment-level or recording-level leakage in all datasets.

The writing contains numerous errors and overclaims, including typos, inconsistent naming between TFM-Token and TFM-Tokenizer, and claims such as 'state-of-the-art' and 'foundation' that are not adequately supported by the experiments.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: discrete, scalable tokenization for EEG, with a clear motivation around frequency structure, channel variability, and the limitations of continuous EEG embeddings.

The proposed TFM-Tokenizer/TFM-Encoder pipeline is technically coherent and well aligned with the problem. Combining STFT-window frequency modeling, raw temporal patches, VQ-style discretization, and masked token prediction is a sensible design.

The empirical evaluation is broader than many EEG representation papers: four clinical EEG datasets are considered, with relevant metrics for imbalanced binary and multiclass settings, five random seeds, and comparisons to strong recent baselines including BIOT and LaBraM.

The reported results are consistently positive. Gains on TUEV, TUAB, CHB-MIT, and IIIC Seizure, while not always large, are directionally consistent and achieved with fewer parameters than several baselines.

The ablations are useful: raw-only vs STFT-only vs joint modeling, masking strategy, position embedding, vocabulary size, and masked token prediction pretraining all help substantiate the architectural choices.

The token-quality analyses and motif visualizations are a valuable addition. They make the paper more than a leaderboard submission and provide some evidence that the learned tokens capture meaningful EEG time-frequency structure.
weaknesses: The strongest claims about scalability, generality, and foundation-model relevance are not fully demonstrated. All training appears to be within a single dataset, and there is no convincing cross-dataset transfer, zero/few-shot adaptation, unseen-channel configuration test, or pretrain-on-many/tasks-then-adapt evaluation.

Novelty is solid but not clearly high. The method is largely a careful combination of known ingredients: STFT features, transformers, VQ tokenization, masking, and EEG pretraining. The paper would benefit from sharper positioning against prior discrete time-series/EEG tokenizers and frequency-domain representation methods.

Baseline fairness is somewhat hard to assess. The paper reproduces baselines, but preprocessing and channel choices differ from LaBraM’s original setup, and the comparison uses single-dataset training rather than the large-scale pretraining regimes that motivate some foundation baselines.

The interpretability evidence remains preliminary. The class-token uniqueness metric is intuitive but not obviously clinically meaningful, and the motif visualization is qualitative without expert validation, quantitative alignment to known EEG biomarkers, or robustness checks.

Some token analyses raise questions. Token utilization is very low relative to the 8192-token vocabulary, and the class-unique token percentages are also small; the paper argues this is compactness, but it could also indicate underuse or codebook inefficiency.

Reproducibility is incomplete from the manuscript alone. Hyperparameters and splits are described, but there is no clear statement about code/model release, computational cost, training time, or hardware requirements.

The evaluation would be stronger with statistical significance testing, calibration/error analysis, per-class results for the clinically important datasets, and sensitivity to window size/STFT settings.

The writing is generally understandable but has several typos and imprecise claims, and some conclusions are stronger than the evidence, especially around foundation models and clinical interpretability.

strengths: The paper identifies a timely and important problem: reusable EEG tokenization, rather than treating short continuous segments as tokens or using a tokenizer only as a pretraining target.

The proposed single-channel time-frequency motif tokenizer is well motivated for heterogeneous EEG settings, and the architecture combines sensible ingredients: STFT windows, frequency-local encoding, temporal modeling, VQ quantization, and masked reconstruction.
The empirical evaluation is broad for this domain, covering TUEV, TUAB, CHB-MIT, IIIC Seizure, and an out-of-domain ear-EEG sleep staging setting.
Results are generally strong, especially on TUEV and IIIC under multi-dataset pretraining, with consistent gains in several core metrics over BIOT, LaBraM, EEGPT, and conventional baselines.
The paper includes useful ablations on raw versus spectral input, masking strategy, positional embeddings, vocabulary size, downstream transformer depth, and masked token prediction.

The token analysis is a valuable addition: class-token uniqueness, retrieval consistency, token utilization, spectral entropy, and qualitative motif examples make the representation claims more interpretable than a pure benchmark paper.
The method is parameter-efficient relative to several baselines, which is practically meaningful for EEG deployment settings.
weaknesses: The novelty is meaningful but somewhat incremental: the core components are mostly adaptations of VQ-VAE-style tokenization, masked modeling, STFT features, and transformer encoders to EEG, and the paper could better distinguish what is technically new from a strong engineering combination.

Some headline claims are overstated. For example, the tokenizer is described as consistently improving foundation models, but detailed results show mixed behavior across metrics, including drops in balanced accuracy for some BIOT-TFM settings and mixed CHB-MIT results.

The comparison to large foundation models is not fully clean. LaBraM is reproduced with a much smaller pretraining corpus than the original, while some other baselines use reported results or released weights; this makes the fairness of the strongest comparative claims hard to assess.
The gains are sometimes modest relative to standard deviations, particularly in the single-dataset setting, and the paper does not consistently report statistical tests across all main comparisons.

The contribution of the tokenizer itself is partially confounded with the downstream transformer, masked token prediction stage, hyperparameter tuning, and preprocessing choices. The ablations help, but a more direct controlled comparison using identical downstream models and training budgets would strengthen the causal claim.
The cross-device ear-EEG experiment is promising but small, with only 10 subjects and a single subject split; it supports feasibility more than broad claims of device-agnostic scalability.

The interpretability analysis is suggestive but limited. Class-token uniqueness scores are very small in absolute value, the Jaccard retrieval metric is preliminary, and the qualitative motif examples are not enough to establish clinical interpretability.
Reproducibility is weakened by the apparently missing code URL in the manuscript, despite claims that code and pretrained weights are available.

Several writing and presentation issues remain, including typos, formatting artifacts, and imprecise language such as calling ear-EEG a different brain-signal type rather than a different EEG acquisition setup.

strengths: The paper targets a meaningful problem: EEG tokenization for foundation-model-style pipelines, especially under varying channel/device configurations.
The proposed single-channel, time-frequency VQ tokenizer is a plausible engineering design and is reasonably well motivated by EEG spectral structure.
The empirical section is broader than many submissions in this area, covering TUEV, TUAB, IIIC, CHB-MIT, and an ear-EEG sleep-staging transfer setting.
The paper includes several useful ablations, including raw-only versus spectrogram-only tokenizers, masking variants, vocabulary size, masked-token pretraining, and position embeddings.
The idea of using learned discrete EEG motifs as reusable inputs to multiple downstream models is potentially useful for compact, device-flexible EEG modeling.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited for a top-tier AI venue. The method is largely a combination of STFT features, VQ-style discretization, masking/reconstruction, and transformer encoders, without a clearly new algorithmic insight beyond adapting known components to EEG.

Some central claims are overstated. The paper claims consistent superiority, but on CHB-MIT with multiple-dataset pretraining BIOT has substantially higher balanced accuracy than TFM-Tokenizer, while TFM-Tokenizer mainly improves AUC-PR/AUROC. The text does not adequately qualify these mixed results.

The evaluation is not fully convincing because comparisons mix reported numbers, reproduced baselines, and differently pretrained models. The fairness of the LaBraM, BIOT, EEGPT, and NeuroLM comparisons is hard to assess, especially when original large-scale pretraining is replaced or unavailable.

The token interpretability analysis is weak. Metrics such as class-token uniqueness and Jaccard retrieval are heuristic, and the spectral-entropy analysis of token sequences is questionable because arbitrary VQ code indices do not have an inherent frequency ordering suitable for Fourier analysis.

The scalability/device-agnostic claim rests on one small ear-EEG dataset with 10 subjects and only fine-tuning evaluation. This is not enough to support broad claims about cross-device generalization.

The ablations do not fully isolate important design choices, such as the value of discrete tokens versus continuous latent embeddings, VQ versus alternative quantizers, learned STFT/multiresolution spectral features, codebook size under controlled capacity, or the effect of the downstream transformer architecture.

The paper provides limited statistical treatment. Some p-values are mentioned selectively, but many comparisons have overlapping standard deviations or small absolute gains, and significance is not systematically reported across datasets and metrics.

Reproducibility is weaker than claimed: the code link in the manuscript appears blank, and important implementation details such as data filtering choices, exact baseline tuning budgets, leakage controls across TUH-derived datasets, and hyperparameter search ranges are insufficiently specified.

The writing and presentation contain numerous formatting and clarity issues, including missing repository URL, cramped tables, inconsistent claims, and typographical problems, which reduce confidence in the care of the submission.
Overall, the paper has a reasonable application contribution but does not provide enough novelty, rigor, or reliable evidence for acceptance at a selective AI conference.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: principled tokenization for EEG foundation models, moving beyond treating fixed signal segments as tokens.
The proposed TFM-Tokenizer is conceptually appealing: single-channel, model-agnostic, and based on time-frequency motif learning via VQ-style discrete codes.
The empirical evaluation is fairly broad, covering TUEV, TUAB, IIIC-Seizure, CHB-MIT, and an out-of-domain ear-EEG sleep staging setting.
Results are consistently strong for the authors' own lightweight downstream transformer, with especially notable gains on TUEV and IIIC under multi-dataset pretraining.
The paper includes useful ablations on temporal vs spectral inputs, masking strategy, position embeddings, vocabulary size, and downstream transformer depth.
The plug-and-play experiments with BIOT and LaBraM strengthen the claim that the tokenizer can improve existing EEG foundation model pipelines.
weaknesses: The novelty is meaningful but not fully decisive: the method combines familiar ingredients such as STFT features, masking, transformers, and VQ tokenization, and the paper could better distinguish what is fundamentally new versus a well-engineered adaptation to EEG.
Some claims of consistent improvement are overstated. For example, BIOT-TFM decreases balanced accuracy in several settings, and CHB-MIT results are mixed depending on the metric.
The comparison to foundation models is somewhat complicated by different pretraining corpora and reproduced variants; the fairness of the baseline setup is not always fully convincing.
The interpretability analysis is interesting but still preliminary. Metrics such as class-token uniqueness and Jaccard retrieval are ad hoc, and the qualitative motif examples are small-scale.
The scalability claim is promising but supported by only one small ear-EEG dataset with 10 subjects, so the evidence for broad cross-device generalization remains limited.
The reproducibility statement appears to have a missing code URL in the manuscript text, and some implementation details would need the released repository to verify.
Clinical relevance and deployment risks are not deeply discussed, despite the paper targeting medical EEG classification tasks.
